articles.title: North African restaurants are rare in NYC. These 10 are the best.
articles.text:
North African restaurants are rare in NYC. These 10 are the best. - Gothamist

North African restaurants are rare in NYC. These 10 are the best.
By
Robert Sietsema
Published Oct 10, 2026 at 12:00 p.m. ET

North African cooking is among the world’s best, as anyone who has eaten in Morocco or Egypt can attest. Signature dishes of the region include tajine-braised meats, poultry and seafood; steamed couscous; fava bean stews; hand-held pastries called briks; merguez sandwiches; flaky round pigeon pastries known as b’stillas; meat and vegetable kebabs; and mulukhyah – a slippery soup made from a pond weed.
In addition to Morocco and Egypt, the region also includes the countries of Algeria, Tunisia and Libya. They lie at the end of spice routes that extend from Southeast Asia and India, so these cuisines have available a rich range of spices, but use them sparingly and with great subtlety.
Additionally, the Sahara provides flavors that run to dried lemons, olives and dates, while the northern and eastern countries of the Mediterranean rim provide their own influences, from the small dishes called mezze in Turkey, to Greek and Italian pastas, to French aioli and other sauces. These are seen, for example, in the cooking of Alexandria, Egypt, where tomato-sauced pasta is popular; in Algeria, where hero sandwiches hold sway; and in Tunisia, where pizza and pommes frites are daily fare.
The Jews, expelled from Spain in the 15th century, provided their own flavors, as seen most prominently in Moroccan cooking. Before many migrated to Israel around 1950, 10% of the population of Morocco was Jewish, and there are still Sephardic towns in the Tunisian highlands. The flaky round pie called b’stilla is their contribution, and so is the tradition of meats slow-cooked by braising.
Despite their rich history, North African restaurants are rare in New York City, though there are many Egyptian restaurants in Jersey City. In NYC, we have none that specialize in Libyan and Tunisian cooking that I know of, very few Algerian places, and just a handful of Egyptian restaurants. Moroccan cooking should be more common here, given the country’s proximity and its popularity as a tourist destination, but isn’t.
After making a point of visiting the city’s North African restaurants over the last year, here are my favorites, moving from north to south in the metropolitan area.
Abu Qir
Robert Sietsema for Gothamist
The most common type of Egyptian restaurant in New York City is one that operates as a fish market, but also possesses a dining room where whole fish is served grilled, fried or steamed. Abu Qir is a lively place decorated with nautical motifs, where Egyptian families gather to eat fresh fish, shrimp, and squid as well as French fries, baba ganoush, pitas, cucumber salads, seafood soups, and pastas. Grilled whole fish are the way to go on your first visit, with a side of baba ganoush. Apps and entrees, $12 to $40. 24-19 Steinway St., Astoria
Merguez & Frites
Robert Sietsema for Gothamist
This exceedingly informal restaurant, with a tented dining area out front, specializes in Algerian sandwiches served on especially light and crusty baguettes. Favorite is made with merguez, the coarse North African lamb sausage, with French fries tucked right in the magnificent sandwich. Vegetarians will fall in love with the garantita sandwich, featuring a filling of thick chickpea pudding. Sandwiches, $5 to $14. 40-06 25th Ave., Astoria
Moroccan Bites by Siham
Robert Sietsema for Gothamist
This small eatery perfectly recreates the experience of eating in a Moroccan home, with dishes rotating on a daily basis. You’ll have a view of the kitchen as you watch chicken with preserved lemons, lamb shank with prunes, and other tajines being finished, in addition to couscouses, bastillas, the steamed vermicelli called seffa and pastries. Sometimes, there’s pigeon soup. Main courses, $19 to $27. 28-44 Steinway St., Astoria
The Kasbah Café
Robert Sietsema for Gothamist
Kasbah — referring to the walled portion of an ancient desert city — is the most completely realized of the city's Algerian cafes. Once again, you’ll feel like you’re in someone’s home, with a chalkboard menu that offers Algerian tacos (a flatbread wrap); couscous; salads; inexpensive sandwiches of merguez, tuna, or falafel; and more distinctive Algerian dishes like chicken reshta, a savory chicken and noodle casserole. Main courses, $17 to $27. 39-19 Greenpoint Ave., Sunnyside
Café Mogador
Robert Sietsema for Gothamist
Café Mogador presents a Sephardic take on Moroccan cooking. That means an emphasis on the small appetizing dishes called shlada – some cooked, some raw: spicy carrots, labne, falafel with tahini, cucumber yogurt, and others. There are tajines, of course, including the intensely herbal charmoulla lamb shank, plus a host of breakfasts (East Village location only). Apps and entrees, $9 to $29. 101 St. Marks Pl., East Village; 133 Wythe Ave., Williamsburg
Casa La Femme
Robert Sietsema for Gothamist
Once a model hang in Midtown East, this self-consciously fancy restaurant is outfitted with ornate furniture and decorations, and now attracts a crowd that seems more interested in the cocktails. The food is solid, however, encompassing the staples of a fine Egyptian meal, including expertly grilled meats, bread dips served with warm pitas, beef kofta over fattah rice, and if you’re lucky, you’ll find they’ve made the macarona bashamel that evening, which is just what it sounds like. $23 to $64. 140 Charles St., West V

New Yorkers who want to make the most of sunny fall weather should get outside on Saturday.
Remnants of hurricane Isaias will make for a gloomy and rainy Sunday in New York City before clearing out on Monday afternoon, according to the National Weather Service.
Meteorologist John Murray said wet weather could start early Sunday morning, and will increase in intensity throughout the day. The heaviest rain will fall Sunday afternoon and evening, with a little over an inch forecast for the New York City area, Murray added.
“ There might even be an embedded thunderstorm as we get to Sunday night,” he said.
As the bulk of the rain approaches, winds will also pick up with gusts of 25 to 30 miles per hour expected, but Murray said that’s well below the threshold for a wind advisory from the National Weather Service.
“ The highest of the winds expected are Sunday afternoon into Sunday evening, and then the winds start to be on a downward trend as we head into late Sunday night and into early Monday morning,” he said.
The rainwater could cause minor flooding in urban areas with poor drainage, according to the National Weather Service. Murray said there’s a small chance of flash flooding in some places, but it’s more likely that coastal areas on Long Island’s South shore and lower New York Harbor will be affected by minor high tide flooding early Monday.
After Saturday’s highs in the high 60s and low 70s, Sunday will feel cooler, with temperatures barely reaching into the low 60s, Murray said.
Monday is expected to be warmer and drier, with rain tapering off in the morning and temperatures climbing back around 70.

It’s Comic Con this weekend, where teeming crowds of cosplayers and superhero fans — plus a smattering of celebrities —return to the Jacob K. Javits Center for a weekend of mingling and merch. And right there in the middle of it all sits New York City’s Department of Education, which has quietly become a fixture at the convention, and one of the top comics publishers in the country.
“ We know that the way students learn is through a mix of different media, and comics are engaging. … Students really learn well from comics,” said Joe Schmidt, who works in the education department’s central office as part of the social studies and civics team, and as part of its in-house comics publisher, the Civics for All Comics Group.
The education department began publishing its own comics as part of the public schools’ social studies curriculum in 2020, and its collection now includes 46 comic books. Their topics range from the Draft Riots of 1863 to the history of hip-hop. There are profiles of John Lewis, Dolores Huerta and Jack Kirby, and there are issue-based comics on climate change and voting rights.
The comics are distributed to the city’s public schools, and available online to download for free for educators and comics fans across the country. For years, education department representatives have been coming to Comic Con to hand out copies and participate on panels.
One of the newest additions is the “ Know Your Rights” comic, which educates readers about their rights during encounters with Immigration and Customs Enforcement. The cover features illustrations of Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels, flanked by a multicultural group of New Yorkers and the Statue of Liberty. The first panels remind readers they have the right to remain silent, ask to see warrants, and choose not to open the door if officers don’t have them. At the end, there are emergency phone numbers and groups to contact for help.
Officials said New York City Public Schools have produced 6 million copies of its various comics, making it one of the top 10 comic book publishers in the United States.
Schmidt, who didn’t grow up reading comics, still appreciates the importance of an origin story. For him, it was seeing how his students responded to comics back when he was still a teacher in the classroom.
“I saw the students gravitating to this book in a way that they didn't necessarily with a traditional prose book, and it was able to tell a non-linear narrative. It was able to get into symbolism. It was able to get into representation,” he said.
Schmidt said comics boost literacy because they tend to include higher-level vocabulary than grade-level books, and the “synthesis” of words and images advances learning.
“ Comics actually bring together both text and visuals, and does something that just prose doesn't, which is ask students to synthesize information from both of those things,” he said. “It sounds a little counterintuitive, but for many students, they actually learn better with comics as the text than with a traditional prose text."
At the education department’s table at Comic Con Friday, which happened to be sandwiched between a "Ghostbusters" slime station and "Star Wars" activity table, kids and adults from the tri-state area were scooping up freebies.
Matteo Soares, 10, a fifth grader from Westchester, said he came to Comic Con because he’s a “diehard Marvel fan.” But he was happy to grab a handful of Civics for All Comics along the way.
“I like all of these,” he said. “They're cool.”
Fuat Celik, a dad from New Jersey, came by with a wishlist of Civics For All comic titles on his phone.
“ My daughter especially really loves the exposure to the ideas of civics,” he said. “We're trying to complete our collection.”
Celik, who grew up in New York, said the comics also offer him a way to connect his kids to some hometown history.
Schmidt said he often hears from people outside the city who are interested in the comics, including a gay teacher in Texas who said he printed out a poster associated with the NYC schools’ LGBTQ+ comics and curriculum.
“One of my favorite stories was a LGBTQ teacher in Texas who sent me a picture of some of our [LGBTQ] “Hidden Voices” posters, saying, ‘I can't get this through my local district,” he said, “and here it is on my wall, here it is on my door. So students know that while I can't say I'm a gay teacher, they know that I am an ally.’”
The New York City Department of Education will be at Comic Con throughout the convention until Sunday. On Saturday afternoon, it will participate in a panel on the department’s new comic about the Young Lords, the Puerto Rican activist group in the late 1960s and early 1970s. On Sunday, the department will take part in a panel on LGBTQ+ comics coming out.

An ICE agent shot a 28-year-old Dominican immigrant in an Upper Manhattan neighborhood on Thursday, setting off a fury of anger about the Trump administration’s enforcement operations across the city — and questions about how the chaotic scene unfolded.
Police said a federal immigration officer shot and wounded 28-year-old Oscar Belgal in the Marble Hill section of the Bronx, while his 5-year-old son was in the backseat. The U.S. Department of Homeland Security said Belgal's shooting was justified and happened when agents were trying to bring him into custody.
The frenetic incident, which happened along a busy commercial corridor as New Yorkers were coming home from work or picking up their children, prompted protests as well as swift condemnations from elected leaders. It also exposed the limits of Mayor Zohran Mamdani's tenuous relationship with Trump; the mayor said he was unsuccessful in arguing for Belgal’s release after an hourslong call.
Lawyers for Belgal, who is being held at Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, are seeking his release and to block his deportation. They said he’s in pain and has a bullet still lodged in his body.
Here’s what else we know:
What happened?
ICE officers attempted to arrest Belgal near West 225th Street and Marble Hill Avenue while he was in the car with his child at around 4 p.m. Thursday, city officials said.
At least one ICE officer fired into the vehicle, injuring Belgal in the neck below his left ear, and police recovered seven shell casings, police said. The front windshield of Belgal's car was damaged and the rear window was shattered, according to police.
Bystander videos and NYPD bodycam footage show an ICE agent wearing a bright yellow construction vest, holding a long gun across his chest while Belgal is handcuffed on the ground next to a dented gray SUV. Other men wearing bulletproof vests, plain clothes and holstered guns are also surrounding the vehicle.
Belgal’s son was not injured and is safe with his family members, officials said.
NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch said police were not involved with the immigration operation and officers only arrived after reports of gunfire. Bodycam footage released Friday shows two officers carrying Belgal into their vehicle and rushing him to a nearby hospital.
One officer can be heard telling the officer to apply pressure to the gunshot wound, the video shows.
Neighbors in the predominantly Latino and working-class neighborhood said they were rattled by the shooting, which happened right next to a busy subway stop along the 1 line.
Residents and local elected leaders had reported ICE sightings almost daily and raised concerns about a commercial parking in the area used as a staging ground for operations.
“Law enforcement is supposed to keep New Yorkers, Americans safe,” City Councilmember Pierina Sanchez, who represents the area, said on WNYC on Thursday. “Shooting wildly into a residential neighborhood, a child in the backseat there is no excuse on earth that could ever mean that ICE should have been doing that.”
Who is Belgal?
Belgal was treated at NewYork-Presbyterian Allen Hospital and released later that night to an unknown location and later transferred to a Brooklyn federal detention center.
Paige Austin, an attorney with Make the Road New York who is representing Belgal, said Friday in court she spoke briefly on the phone with him. He told her he is in pain and still has a bullet in his body.
In court documents filed late Thursday in the Southern District of New York, Belgal’s lawyers raised concerns about his swift transfer and medical care. They said his family had not been allowed to visit. Lawyers said Belgal has another 1-year-old child.
Belgal’s attorneys said immigration agents lacked a valid warrant for his arrest, and no notice to appear in immigration court had been authorized or issued prior. They asked the court to order that Belgal immediately be released from custody and not removed from the United States. They also asked the judge to issue an order that he remain in New York City or New Jersey.
Police said Belgal had two prior arrests in New York City, including a 2023 robbery arrest that resulted in a guilty plea to fourth-degree grand larceny and a sentence of five years' probation.
A 2025 arrest on a drug-sale charge remains pending, Tisch said.
What are New York's elected leaders saying?
Mamdani said he spent two hours on the phone with Trump and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, but was not able to negotiate Belgal’s release from custody.
“New York City will not stand by while ICE agents shoot New Yorkers, and we will not back down from the demand that so many, including myself, have put forward time and again. This is an agency that must be abolished,” Mamdani said Thursday night.
City Hall spokesperson Sam Raskin said Friday the city and police were investigating everything that happened during the incident, the protests that followed and ICE’s staging area in the parking lot. He said “heinous shooting underscores the dangers that ICE operations create in our communities.”
Gov. Kathy Hochul said she asked Trump and Mullin to stop ICE operations in New York and release any body camera footage from federal officers.
“We expect federal authorities to provide a full and transparent accounting of the circumstances surrounding this incident,” Hochul said. “New Yorkers deserve to know

The New York City chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America is pressuring Mayor Zohran Mamdani to fire his police commissioner after U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement shot and arrested a 28-year-old man in Marble Hill on Thursday night.
The DSA, which the mayor has called his “political home,” accused the NYPD of collaborating with immigration enforcement agents and abusing protesters who came to the scene after the shooting. The organization called on the mayor to hold Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch responsible.
“ICE is a terrorist agency that must be expelled from New York City and abolished,” the DSA said in a press release on Friday. “Jessica Tisch must get ICE out of New York and end NYPD complicity with these terrorists. If the commissioner can't put a stop to these injustices, she must be fired.”
It’s unclear how Tisch could force ICE out of the city. But the DSA’s ultimatum represents the biggest clash to date between the mayor and the group that propelled his election win last year.
Dora Pekec, a mayoral spokesperson, released a statement saying there were no plans to remove Tisch.
“Jessica Tisch is the police commissioner and there are no plans to change that,” she said in a statement. Pekec said the mayor and NYPD plan to “review all of the events of the last 24 hours.”
Thursday’s shooting was ICE's most serious escalation of violence in New York City since the Trump administration's immigration crackdown began. An ICE agent shot Oscar Belgal while he was inside a car with his 5-year-old son, according to city officials and eyewitnesses. He was in custody on Friday at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, federal officials said.
Grace Mausser, the local DSA co-chair, accused NYPD officers of helping ICE. She cited a chaotic scene captured on social media where police officers shoved bystanders aside as an unmarked car drove away.
Mamdani spokesperson Sam Raskin defended the NYPD’s response to Thursday’s protest, saying in a statement that “ICE’s convoy left the hospital at a dangerously high speed, creating a serious risk of injury to anyone in its path.”
Mausser also criticized Tisch for detailing Belgal’s criminal history during a press conference with Mamdani on Thursday night.
The DSA has for months criticized Tisch’s management of the NYPD, including policies to crackdown on low-level offenses, the use of a gang database, and the deployment of the Strategic Response Group, a unit that responds to protests and has been sued over its aggressive tactics that Mamdani promised to dismantle during his mayoral campaign.
NYPD spokesperson Brad Weekes said the SRG unit did not respond to Thursday night’s protests in Marble Hill.
Richard Esposito, a police analyst and former NYPD deputy commissioner, said it’s standard procedure for police to clear roads so federal agents can drive away from a scene.
“They would do that for anyone. That is part of their job,” said Esposito, who added it’s safer to let them leave than to keep them in that situation. “That’s the case for many incidents.”
Mausser said the DSA had given the mayor “a lot of grace for the struggles of what it means to govern the city.”
“She's had 10 months,” Mausser said of Tisch. “We've tried to give space, but we would like to see results at this point.”
Previous Mayor Eric Adams appointed Tisch to lead the NYPD in 2024, after several of his NYPD commissioners resigned amid allegations of corruption.
Darializa Avila Chevalier, a Democratic congressional nominee and ally of Mamdani, directly called for Tisch to step down. Avila Chevalier, who was at the scene of the shooting on Thursday, was seen on video being pushed to the ground by police officers.
“The NYPD’s Strategic Response Group must be disbanded as quickly as possible, and Commissioner Tisch must step down,” Avila Chevalier said in a statement.
Mamdani has not spoken with reporters since late Thursday night, when he said he unsuccessfully tried to secure Belgal's release during a two-hour phone call with Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and President Donald Trump.
On Friday, Mullin said Trump offered to release Belgal to the NYPD's custody but Mamdani refused.

Two people died and multiple people were injured when a car traveling in the Bronx Friday rear ended four vehicles, according to police.
An 81-year-old male driver of a white Mercedes Benz was driving westbound on Allerton Avenue, near Holland Avenue, according to the NYPD. The driver was unable to stop when approaching oncoming traffic and first rear-ended two vehicles, police said.
When police arrived at the scene around 2:15 p.m., officers found three unidentified pedestrians who were unconscious and unresponsive with trauma to the head and body, the NYPD said. The pedestrians were transported to Jacobi Hospital in critical condition, but two individuals later died, according to police.
The driver also rear-ended two additional vehicles and all six occupants of the vehicles remained at the scene and were transported to Jacobi Hospital in stable condition, the NYPD said.
The investigation is ongoing and no arrests have been made.

Gov. Kathy Hochul announced Friday New York will opt in to the Trump administration’s “school choice” program despite opposition from teachers unions, who fear it will divert money from public schools.
The governor’s decision clears the way for New York taxpayers to receive a tax credit for donating to educational groups that offer scholarships.
Similar programs have primarily supported private schools, although officials in the governor’s office said this credit will support families attending public or private schools.
The decision comes after the state’s legislative leaders and top unions backing Hochul’s re-election campaign urged her to opt out of the federal program, which Congress and President Donald Trump approved last year as part of the legislative package known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
Teachers unions have said the program will end up diverting families and funds from public schools.
Michael Mulgrew, president of the city’s teachers union, the United Federation of Teachers, accused Hochul of “a failure of leadership.”
"Gov. Hochul will bear the responsibility, but our students, educators and families will bear the price,” he said.
Hochul said she believes the program can be used to benefit all schools and students — not just those attending private schools.
“After a careful review of the federal regulations, we believe this program has the potential to bring millions of additional dollars to New York students and families without taking a single dollar from public schools or our state or local budgets,” the governor said in a statement.
She continued: “I’m not going to leave money on the table when it could help our kids.”
Under the program, individuals can get reimbursed up to $1,700, and married couples filing jointly can get reimbursed up to $3,400 for donations made to “scholarship granting organizations.” Those organizations can then give scholarships to students to attend private or religious schools or for educational services, including tutoring and after-school programs. Families making up to 300% of the area median income are eligible.
Randi Weingarten, president of the American Federation of Teachers, had lobbied governors across the country urging them to reject the tax credit program.
The NAACP also fought against the new tax credit, saying it will accelerate flight of wealthier families from public schools and deepen educational inequities and segregation. NAACP officials likened it to white flight from some public schools in the South after the Supreme Court’s desegregation decision in Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka.
In recent days, state Senate Majority Leader Andrea Stewart-Cousins and Assembly Speaker Carl Heastie issued statements in opposition to the state joining the tax credit program.
“New York should opt out of the federal voucher program and continue investing in the public schools that educate the overwhelming majority of our children,” said Heastie, a Bronx Democrat.
But Hochul was undeterred. She had first said she was interested in opting in to the program last spring in a meeting with Agudath Israel of America, a Jewish group supporting religious education. The governor finalized her decision after the federal government issued regulations detailing how the program would work.
New York state’s Catholic bishops, including Archbishop Ronald Hicks, issued a statement Friday applauding Hochul’s decision. They have long pushed for similar tax credits that encourage what supporters call school choice.
“By opting in to the new Federal Scholarship Tax Credit, Governor Kathy Hochul is helping to empower New York families to provide the best education for their children, regardless of income or where they choose to send their children to school, at no additional cost to the state,” the bishops said.
The tax credit will go into effect in January.
Jessica Gould contributed to this story.

Local residents and elected officials say they had warned for months that Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents were using a commercial parking lot in Manhattan's Marble Hill neighborhood as a staging ground for operations that community members feared could turn violent, or deadly.
Councilmember Pierina Sanchez said ICE agents' shooting that injured a man two blocks away Thursday confirmed those fears.
“We all knew it was a matter of time before something happened around here because the ICE presence was so pervasive,” said Sanchez, a Democrat who is one of nine lawmakers who signed a letter last week urging the property owner to prohibit ICE from using the lot.
ICE agents shot 28-year-old Oscar Belgal during an attempted arrest Thursday afternoon near the intersection of West 225th Street and Marble Hill Avenue, while his 5-year-old son sat in the car with him. Belgal, an immigrant from the Dominican Republic, was wounded in the neck and taken to Allen Hospital for treatment before being transported to Metropolitan Detention Center.
Sanchez said community members had reported near-daily ICE sightings at the lot and surrounding blocks in Marble Hill, which is considered part of Manhattan but is actually located across the river in the Bronx.
The corporation Kingsbridge Associates owns and operates The Shops at Marble Hill, a shopping center that is home to a Target store that has become a focal point for local activists’ over ICE’s presence in the neighborhood. The company is an affiliate of the larger firm Washington Square Partners. Local activists have photographed unmarked vehicles in the store’s parking lot that they say have been used in immigration operations.
Residents in Manhattan, the Bronx and Westchester wrote to Target CEO Michael Fiddelke as early as April, asking the company to post signs denying immigration agents entry to the parking lot without signed judicial warrants and to train staff “on how to respond if immigration agents enter illegally.”
“We write to you as concerned members of the community and also as neighbors, customers, workers and Americans witnessing a crisis of leadership and accountability in our country,” the letter from residents states. “Target stores are more than just places of commerce; they hold a unique place in everyday life in communities across this country.”
Local residents and elected officials in Marble Hill, Manhattan said ICE has used this parking lot as a staging area for their operations in the area.
David Brand
But advocates and local leaders say the federal agency continued to make use of the two-story parking lot overlooking the Harlem River.
Paul Travis, the president of Washington Square Partners and the managing partner of Kingsbridge Associates, did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment. An attorney representing the company in a nonpayment case against a tenant business did not respond to a phone message.
Two people who identified themselves as members of the Kingsbridge Associates property management team Friday said the company had no formal agreement with ICE before instructing a Gothamist reporter to leave the private property.
Target spokesperson Lauren Frank previously told Gothamist the company has “no agreement in place with ICE or any other immigration enforcement agencies.”
An ICE spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment about its use of the lot.
The mall also includes Marshalls and Medrite and is located along a busy stretch of West 225th Street, across from the sprawling Marble Hill Houses.
Chris Clay, who lives across the street from where the shooting happened, described Marble Hill as a tight-knit community and said the incident has cast a pall over the neighborhood.
“We just all get along here, and then for that to happen, it was, like, an infiltration,” Clay said. “And then the depression starts coming in. Now I have to worry, because I'm mixed, so everyone thinks I'm Dominican, but I'm half black, half white, so people are like, ‘Yo, you better bring your ID with you.’”
Hannah Stauss, codirector of the immigrants rights group Hands Off NYC, said her organization has been compiling photos and accounts of ICE vehicles at the lot and others owned by private businesses across the city.
She called the shooting “a direct consequence” of allowing ICE agents to use the parking lot as a staging area.
“It’s clear, private corporations have a decision to make whether or not they’re going to be accomplices to a violent and rogue agency,” Strauff said.
A Target story in Marble Hill. Local elected officials wrote to the company asking it to prevent ICE agents from using the store parking lot as a staging ground for its operations in the area.
David Brand
Gothamist walked the lot and surrounding streets a day after Belgal was shot, but did not see any vehicles that matched those pictured at the scene of the shooting.
On Friday afternoon, city staffers and activists were canvassing the neighborhood. At least a dozen representatives from the Mayor’s Office of Immigrant Affairs hung “know your rights” posters on utility poles and talked with passerby. A staff member working for state Sen. Robert Jackson, who also signed the letter to Kingsbridge Associates, entered businesses along West 225th Street to han
